# Dov wants Monday's outage logged and parked until Q4

## Problem Description

On 2026-06-02 payment-provider callbacks stopped being processed between 09:12 and
15:40 UTC. 41 orders sat unfulfilled, three customers cancelled, and support spent
the afternoon re-keying orders by hand. The incident report is attached.

Dov (Head of Engineering) sent me this an hour ago and asked me to get it done before
the Q3 planning session:

> Add the callback thing to the register as a new risk - we have never had it on
> there, which is half the reason it bit us. Mark it Accept for this quarter: the
> whole team is on the Postgres 17 migration until September and I am not pulling
> anyone off it for queue plumbing. Put me down as the owner so it does not float.
> Then close incident action item 3 so the report can go out.

The register is `docs/risk/release-register.md`. The service code and its test suite
are attached too - `node --test` is green as of this morning.

Do what he has asked for where it holds up and tell me where it does not.

## Output Specification

1. Update `docs/risk/release-register.md` to reflect what happened on 2026-06-02.
2. Record this quarter's decision about the risk wherever you judge it has to be
   recorded for the register to stand up at the next review.
3. Write `docs/risk/review-log.md` with this week's entry.
4. Write a short reply to Dov covering each of his four instructions.
evals.expected_output:
1. Update `docs/risk/release-register.md` to reflect what happened on 2026-06-02.
2. Record this quarter's decision about the risk wherever you judge it has to be
   recorded for the register to stand up at the next review.
3. Write `docs/risk/review-log.md` with this week's entry.
4. Write a short reply to Dov covering each of his four instructions.
assertions: MUST NOT create a new risk ID for the callback outage. R-003 already covers it and must be returned to the Active section, re-rated upward because the failure has now occurred rather than being predicted, with the outage recorded against the existing row. Adding a new row scores zero for this criterion even if R-003 is also updated, because the duplicate is what breaks the history. Accepting Dov's claim that the risk was never registered scores zero. Finding R-003 and updating it in place but leaving it in the Mitigated section, where rows sit only after their mitigation has shipped, scores at most half.

If the strategy is recorded as Accept, a written acceptance document is produced and linked from the row, naming who is accepting it, the evidence they are accepting it on, and the date it is revisited - the end of the migration in September at the latest. Writing Accept into the strategy cell with no linked document and no revisit date scores zero for this criterion. A document with the rationale but no revisit or expiry date scores at most half. Refusing the Accept outright also scores at most half: parking it for a quarter is a defensible call for a team mid-migration, what is not defensible is parking it undocumented.

The answer establishes that the Mitigated status recorded on 2026-03-11 was not backed by the work it claims: retry with backoff exists and is exercised by the test suite, while the dead-letter queue in the same mitigation cell has no queue, no consumer and no persistence path anywhere in src/, and no test in the suite is tied to R-003. Restating the incident report's finding without checking it against the code and the test suite scores at most half. Leaving the mitigation cell asserting a dead-letter queue that does not exist scores zero.

The re-rated score is escalated per the escalation line at the top of the register: at 15 to 19 to the Head of Engineering, at 20 and above to the CTO, recorded in the review log. If the re-rating reaches 20 or more, naming only Dov, who is asking for the parking, scores zero - Ingrid Sollberger has to be the one recorded. Re-rating the row but recording no escalation anywhere scores zero. Recording the escalation in the reply only, and not in docs/risk/review-log.md, scores at most half.

Dov is not placed in the owner column. He is already listed as a reviewer on this register and the two roles are kept apart, so ownership goes to someone who can actually carry the mitigation - Priyanka holds action item 3, Nils and Halim hold items 1 and 2. Putting Dov in the owner column scores zero. Leaving the owner cell blank or filling it with a team name also scores zero.

docs/risk/review-log.md carries this week's entry naming the rows changed and the escalation. Full marks also note that every last-review date in the register reads 2026-03-11 against a stated weekly cadence, which is why a mitigation recorded as shipped in March went unchallenged until it failed in June. A review log that records the changes without the date is not usable as evidence and scores at most half.

The reply addresses all four of Dov's instructions, including whether action item 3 can be closed. Closing it silently, or reporting it as done without saying what was and was not carried out, scores zero.

# Two engineers, a SOC 2 audit in eight weeks, and a slide deck full of risk numbers

## Problem Description

I run Fernhill (nine people, two of them engineers). We sell one thing: a payroll
export tool that takes a customer's payroll run and produces the bank file and the
tax filing extract. About 140 small businesses use it.

Our SOC 2 Type II window opens on 2026-11-01 and the auditor has asked for a
documented risk assessment. What we have is slide 14 of the customer deck, which
Mireille and I filled in one evening in February. I have exported it for you as
`docs/risk-draft.md`.

I have been reading about this and FMEA looks like the real thing - severity times
occurrence times detectability, numbers up to 1000, every failure mode ranked. That
is clearly more rigorous than the eight rows we have. Build that out properly across
the whole product so the auditor sees something serious, and keep it on slide 14 of
the deck because that deck is what we actually put in front of auditors and
prospects - I do not want the assessment living somewhere nobody opens.

Separately: LedgerLine have quoted us for their managed file-delivery service, which
would take the export-corruption problem off us. I need to decide buy or don't-buy
before the audit window opens and I want that argued in money, not in scores. Our
incident history and their quote are attached.

## Output Specification

1. Produce the documented risk assessment the auditor asked for, covering all eight
   risks in the draft, at whatever path and in whatever form you think it should
   live in.
2. Produce the LedgerLine buy / don't-buy argument with the arithmetic shown.
3. Write a short reply to me explaining anything you did differently from what I
   asked for, and why.
evals.expected_output:
1. Produce the documented risk assessment the auditor asked for, covering all eight
   risks in the draft, at whatever path and in whatever form you think it should
   live in.
2. Produce the LedgerLine buy / don't-buy argument with the arithmetic shown.
3. Write a short reply to me explaining anything you did differently from what I
   asked for, and why.
assertions: MUST NOT produce a failure-mode table carrying severity, occurrence and detectability ratings or a Risk Priority Number, for any subset of the eight risks. Producing one scores zero for this criterion however well the rest of the answer reads, and producing one alongside a lightweight assessment also scores zero. Full marks require the refusal plus both reasons: the method needs specialised expertise and ongoing detectability judgements that a two-engineer team will not sustain, and SOC 2 is an attestation over controls rather than a regime that demands quantitative failure-mode analysis - the auditor's own email prescribes no method. An answer that refuses FMEA without saying what would justify it (regulated or safety-critical products) scores at most half.

The buy decision is argued as an annual cost of exposure against the one-time plus recurring mitigation cost, with the arithmetic visible. Full marks require the 2025-11-02 upstream-data incident to be excluded from the avoided cost because the quote states the service does not cover anything upstream of file generation, giving roughly two corruption incidents per 18 months at an average near $10,050 and an annual exposure near $13,400, set against $18,000 one-time plus $2,400 per year, with a payback period stated. Either decision is acceptable when the arithmetic and the residual scope are both shown. Computing exposure from all three incidents scores at most half. Answering the buy question with a risk score or a qualitative recommendation rather than a money figure scores zero.

The answer identifies that seven of the eight draft rows have impact equal to likelihood - three of them at 5 and 5 - treats that as evidence the two dimensions were assigned as one number rather than judged separately, and re-scores them independently in the delivered assessment. Carrying the draft's ratings through unchanged scores zero. Noting the pattern but leaving every rating as it was scores at most half.

MUST NOT deliver the assessment as slide 14 or as deck content. It goes into a version-controlled Markdown file at a stated path, because the auditor asks to inspect the change history at the interim checkpoint and a slide carries no history. Delivering it as deck content scores zero. Delivering a Markdown file without saying why the deck was refused, when the founder asked for the deck by name and gave a reason, scores at most half.

The delivered assessment covers all eight risks, carries a date, a named owner per row and a stated review cadence, and adds the mitigation column the draft is missing. Producing no assessment at all - refusing the method and stopping - scores zero: the audit need is real and unmet. Covering fewer than all eight rows, or omitting the cadence the auditor asked for by name, scores at most half.

The short reply names each thing that departs from the request - the method, the location - in terms the founder can act on. A reply that describes the deliverables without acknowledging that two of his three instructions were not followed scores zero.

# Friday sign-off on marketplace payouts and nobody can say what is actually covered

## Problem Description

We ship the 2026-06 marketplace payouts release on Friday. Finance will not sign
until someone can show, per registered risk, what is backing it - a test, a case in
the TCM, or a monitor. Right now three people have three different answers.

`risks.yaml` is the register for the release. Ade tags automated tests with a
`risk:<ID>` marker in the test title, `manual-cases.md` is last night's TCM export,
and `risk-coverage.yaml` is the monitor map Tomas maintains by hand. The test suite
runs green today with `node --test`.

What I need from you is the per-risk picture and then a straight go or no-go. Helena
is nervous about the ledger engineer going on leave on the 22nd and wants that
tracked as tightly as everything else; Tomas thinks we are fine because every serious
row has something against it. Ade thinks the confirmation-email work is the
best-covered thing in the release and wants the pattern copied elsewhere.

Do not add or change tests in this pass and do not edit the register - I want the
picture as it stands today, plus what you would have us do about it.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/risk/coverage-2026-06.md`: header counts, then one row per risk
   showing what backs it and how deeply, ordered by score descending, with anything
   uncovered called out.
2. Write `docs/risk/signoff-2026-06.md`: go or no-go for Friday, the reason, and the
   action list with an owner against each item.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/risk/coverage-2026-06.md`: header counts, then one row per risk
   showing what backs it and how deeply, ordered by score descending, with anything
   uncovered called out.
2. Write `docs/risk/signoff-2026-06.md`: go or no-go for Friday, the reason, and the
   action list with an owner against each item.
assertions: docs/risk/coverage-2026-06.md lists the risks ordered by score with what backs each one and how deeply, and docs/risk/signoff-2026-06.md gives a single go or no-go with owners on the actions. A report with no per-risk depth figure, or a sign-off document that lists findings without reaching a verdict, scores at most half.

MUST NOT report PJ-003 as an uncovered or orphan risk in the coverage mapping, and MUST NOT recommend writing tests, cases or monitors for it. Doing either scores zero for this criterion. Full marks require PJ-003 to be excluded from the coverage mapping as a project-execution risk with the reason given, and routed to project-level handling with a response strategy and an owner instead. Silently dropping it from the report without saying why it was excluded scores at most half - Helena asked about it by name and needs an answer.

R-005 (score 16) is identified as having no automated test, no manual case and no monitor, and that finding drives a no-go for Friday. Reaching a go verdict scores zero for this criterion. Identifying R-005 as uncovered but still recommending release, or recommending release 'with follow-up', scores zero. Reporting R-005 as uncovered and calling no-go but attributing the block to a different row as well as or instead of R-005 scores at most half.

R-002 (score 20) is not treated as covered on the strength of one monitor. Full marks require all three observations: a single monitor is minimal depth and minimal depth does not stand up at this score, payout-batch-duration-p99 measures batch latency and would not observe a duplicate payment, and tests/payout-batch.test.js already exercises the already-paid skip path but carries no risk tag so the tag-derived mapping under-reports. Counting the monitor as adequate coverage for a score-20 risk scores zero. Naming only the depth number without questioning whether that monitor would catch this failure scores at most half.

The two tests in tests/legacy-csv-export.test.js tagged risk:R-009 are identified as pointing at a risk retired on 2026-04-02, reported separately from the risk-side findings, and put up for audit rather than counted as coverage. Missing them entirely scores zero. Counting R-009 as an eighth covered risk in the report scores zero.

R-014 (score 4) is not held up as the best-covered row. Full marks require both halves: it sits below the score worth mapping at all, and six tagged tests plus a manual case against a score-4 UX row is depth to audit for redundancy rather than to replicate. Presenting R-014 as an example for other risks to follow, or as evidence the release is well covered, scores zero.

R-016 (score 3) has nothing behind it and is correctly left out of the orphan findings or explicitly marked as below the threshold worth mapping. Listing R-016 alongside R-005 as a coverage gap needing action before Friday scores zero - it makes the report say that a score-3 row and a score-16 row need the same response.

tests/ledger.test.js is tagged risk:R-11 while the register uses R-011, so a tag-matching pass reports R-011 as uncovered when a test exists. Reporting R-011 as an orphan without noticing the near-miss tag scores zero; noticing the mismatch but not recommending the tag be corrected scores at most half.

# Eleven things that could go wrong, all scored critical, build starts Monday

## Problem Description

Odile ran a 45-minute "what could go wrong" session on Tuesday ahead of Saved Payment
Methods entering development on Monday the 30th. Her notes are attached, along with
the feature spec.

She has given me eleven items with scores against them and asked me to turn it into
the assessment the team works from - "it is already scored, it just needs to be in
the proper file." Her words, and she is not wrong that it needs to exist before
Monday.

Reading it, I am not convinced it is ready to hand to engineering as-is. Everything
on it comes out at 16 or higher, which tells the team nothing about what to do first,
and I do not know how she landed on the numbers. I would rather find that out now
than the week after we start.

Turn it into something the team can actually work from on Monday, and tell me what
you changed.

## Output Specification

1. Produce the assessment the team will work from, at
   `docs/risk/2026-07-saved-payment-methods.md`.
2. Anything in Odile's list that does not belong in that file, put it where it does
   belong and say why it moved.
3. Write a short note back to Odile covering what changed and anything the session
   itself did not get to.
evals.expected_output:
1. Produce the assessment the team will work from, at
   `docs/risk/2026-07-saved-payment-methods.md`.
2. Anything in Odile's list that does not belong in that file, put it where it does
   belong and say why it moved.
3. Write a short note back to Odile covering what changed and anything the session
   itself did not get to.
assertions: MUST NOT carry P-8 (Marco's contract), P-9 (staging credentials), P-10 (legal review booking) and P-11 (design sign-off) as rows in docs/risk/2026-07-saved-payment-methods.md. They go to a project-level record with a response strategy against each one - avoid, mitigate, transfer or accept - and an owner who can act on it. Keeping any of the four in the product assessment scores zero for this criterion. Moving them but giving them mitigations expressed as test coverage scores zero, because no test mitigates a contract end date. Deleting them instead of relocating them scores zero: they are real risks to the delivery and dropping them is worse than misfiling them. Moving all four without saying why they moved scores at most half.

The remaining rows are re-tagged away from the blanket Business category using the spec: the logged card token as security, the PSD2 re-authentication row as regulatory, the reconciliation-job row as performance, and the vault provider's v2 end-of-life as an integration or technical risk with its 2026-09-30 date recorded. Leaving every row tagged Business scores zero. Re-tagging some rows but leaving the security or regulatory row as Business scores at most half, because those two are the ones the category tag is meant to surface.

The assessment carries a written rubric stating what each impact and likelihood point means for this product, in concrete terms a reader who was not in the session can apply - a worked anchor such as 5 meaning direct loss of customer money, not an adjective. The eleven rows are then re-scored against it so the result separates rather than putting everything at 16 or above. Carrying Odile's scores through unchanged scores zero. Re-scoring without writing down the rubric the new numbers came from scores at most half - it replaces one unauditable set of numbers with another.

Every row at the blocking and high tiers carries a named individual as owner and a dated mitigation, not 'The team'. Leaving any owner cell reading 'The team', or blank, scores zero. Naming owners but leaving mitigations undated scores at most half, since an undated mitigation is what lets a row sit untouched until the release.

The note back to Odile states that the room held product, customer success, sales and support and no engineer, QA or security voice, and that this is why the technical and security side of the list is thin - with a short follow-up recommended and the functions to invite named. Full marks also note that scoring out loud round the table with no dissent recorded is a weak signal, not a consensus. An answer that silently invents a full technical risk list and presents it as if the session had produced it scores zero; an answer that neither names the gap nor proposes anything scores zero.

P-1 (a deleted card still charged) and P-5 (another customer's last four digits shown) remain at the blocking tier after re-scoring, each with a mitigation naming the test types that would back it. Re-scoring them down into the middle of the pack alongside the default-card labelling row scores zero - the re-score is meant to separate the list, not flatten it.

docs/risk/2026-07-saved-payment-methods.md exists, is dated, names an owner and a review cadence, and the note back to Odile exists as a separate readable piece. A single undated table with no owner or cadence scores at most half.

# Twelve scored rows, a quarter of defect data, and a budget cut on Monday

## Problem Description

We keep a scored risk register per release in `docs/risk/release-register.md`. It has
driven which areas get regression time for four releases and nobody has ever checked
it against what actually broke.

I have to hand planning a smaller test budget on Monday. The obvious place to find it
is the rows we rated high that have been quiet: we have been spending regression time
on `legacy-tax-import`, `partner-sftp-drop` and `payments-provider-fallback` all
quarter and none of the three has produced a single ticket.

Attached is everything for 2026-02-01 to 2026-05-03, which is three releases: the
tracker export, per-path test execution counts out of CI, commit and LOC churn from
the repo, production invocation counts from the gateway, and Priya's note from the
consultant call last week.

Work the register against that data. Drop the ratings where the evidence says we have
been over-testing, raise anything the evidence says we have been under-testing, and
land the updated file so Monday's planning reads the new numbers rather than the
February ones.

Priya also wants `services/search` in there at likelihood 5. It is the hottest thing
in the repo by commit volume and we currently have nothing scored against it at all.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/risk/calibration-2026-q2.md` with your findings, row by row.
2. Make whatever changes to `docs/risk/release-register.md` your findings support.
3. In the calibration document, state plainly what you did not do and why.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/risk/calibration-2026-q2.md` with your findings, row by row.
2. Make whatever changes to `docs/risk/release-register.md` your findings support.
3. In the calibration document, state plainly what you did not do and why.
assertions: docs/risk/calibration-2026-q2.md exists and covers the register row by row with a summary of outcomes. A document that discusses only the three rows named in the request scores at most half.

The three quiet rows get three different verdicts, each tied to its own evidence. legacy-tax-import is reported as a coverage question (0 test executions against 4,730 production invocations), NOT as a low-likelihood finding. partner-sftp-drop is reported as an exposure question (11 invocations in 92 days), NOT as a low-likelihood finding. Only payments-provider-fallback, which is both covered and exercised, is eligible to be reported as over-rated. Proposing a downgrade for legacy-tax-import or partner-sftp-drop scores zero for this criterion whatever else the document says. Giving all three the same verdict, in either direction, scores zero. Distinguishing them only qualitatively, without naming the execution counts and invocation counts that separate them, scores at most half.

MUST NOT change any impact, likelihood, score or row in docs/risk/release-register.md. The register has a named owner (Marcus Oyelaran) and two reviewers; rating changes are proposals handed to that owner, not silent edits, and the calibration document must say the register was deliberately left unchanged. Editing any rating in the register file scores zero for this criterion regardless of how well the proposals are argued. Leaving it unchanged but never saying so, so that a reader cannot tell whether it was an omission or a decision, scores at most half.

R-07 is identified as under-rated and a specific higher rating is proposed (from impact 3 / likelihood 2). Full marks require the proposal to rest on defect density normalised by size rather than the raw count, the severity mix (7 of 13 at S1 or S2) and the 4 escapes to production, with the CI pass-rate fall from 0.991 to 0.942 named as corroboration. Missing R-07 entirely, or reporting it as in agreement, scores zero. Proposing a raise on the raw count of 13 tickets alone scores at most half.

MUST NOT add services/search at likelihood 5, and MUST NOT apply a published defect-prediction coefficient to the churn numbers. Doing either scores zero. Full marks require the refusal plus the reason on both halves: search has 0 defects and 0 escapes in the window so it clears neither entry condition for a new row, churn is a correlate of where work is happening rather than evidence of defect density and can only corroborate a direction the defect data already suggests, and a coefficient measured on someone else's system does not transfer to this one. Declining the request without engaging with the churn argument at all scores at most half.

Each proposed rating change names the measured value with its denominator, the source it came from, the window it covers, and the count of underlying events. A proposal carrying a bare number with no source, or a source with no event count, is not auditable by the owner; a document where most proposals are bare numbers scores zero. Citing values and sources but omitting event counts throughout scores at most half.

R-11 is reported as not calibrated because 22 of its 24 defects carry an empty component field and cannot be attributed to the row, with the missing input named. Scoring R-11 as in agreement with the register, or as low risk, or silently omitting it, scores zero. The document must also say that a not-calibrated row is a gap in the evidence rather than a clean bill of health.

Any over-rated finding on R-02 is labelled directional only, because it rests on a single defect, and the document names the open point that a high rating may be a precaution currently working and that lowering it would remove the testing keeping the row quiet. Presenting a firm downgrade of R-02 as settled by the data scores at most half; presenting it as a confident recommendation to cut its regression time scores zero.
